narrative:
The model predicted a 63.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10), while students who were accepted averaged around the middle of their class (5.8). This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling on the bar.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction, modestly pulling the prediction toward passing. At 36, it sits only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, giving the model some reassurance about your ability.

Your first-year class ranking was the third most important factor and again pushed toward denial. Ranking in the second decile is well below the sixth-decile average of accepted students, reinforcing the pattern of academic performance that concerned the model.

Taken together, the model saw your lower class standings as outweighing the relatively solid LSAT, resulting in the elevated risk of bar failure.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic record and bar preparation. Retaking key courses, seeking tutoring, or enrolling in a structured bar-review program could improve both your class rank trajectory and your readiness for the exam. With clearer evidence of progress, a future application would be viewed more favorably. (248 words)
